svg.title: P021 · Top five customers by number of orders
svg.desc: One row per ranked buyer, including fifth-place ties. Nine order rows survive. Orders 17–19 retain ID 99 with NULL customer details. ID 7 has no orders and never enters the ranking. Nine orders form seven buyers. ID 99 contributes 3. IDs 1–6 contribute 1 each. The missing name becomes Unknown customer. Read the grouped buyers. Their counts are 3, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1. The fifth value sets the cutoff at 1. Every buyer reaches 1. All seven appear, including everyone tied for fifth. Sort tied buyers by customer ID.
svg.text: Top five customers by number of orders
One row per ranked buyer, including fifth-place ties.
Customer 99 has three orders and no customer record. Can that ID come first?
A triangle marks an example to follow. Shaded columns show what to read. Double underlines mark the matching keys. SQL excerpts use … for
Nine order rows survive. Orders 17–19 retain ID 99 with NULL customer details. ID 7 has no orders and never enters
Orders LEFT JOIN Customers ON Orders.CustomerID = Customers.CustomerID
Nine orders form seven buyers. ID 99 contributes 3. IDs 1–6 contribute 1 each. The missing name becomes
GROUP BY o.CustomerID, c.FirstName, c.LastName / COUNT(o.OrderID)
Which count is in fifth place?
Read the grouped buyers. Their counts are 3, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1. The fifth value sets the cutoff at 1.
ORDER BY orders_placed DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 4
How many buyers meet that cutoff?
Every buyer reaches 1. All seven appear, including everyone tied for fifth. Sort tied buyers by customer ID.
